title: Appendix A In One Proof
notes: Open by naming the appendix as a proof tool rather than a side topic. The theorem says that a closed form which disappears along the zero section has a local primitive near that section. The route on the slide is the whole argument: build an interval homotopy operator, turn it into a cochain homotopy, apply it to radial contraction in a vector bundle, and then read exactness from the endpoint terms.

title: The Cylinder That Measures Change
notes: Use the cylinder as the geometric source of every sign in the proof. The inclusions j zero and j one pick the two ends of M times R, while the vector field partial t pushes forms from one slice to the next. The formula j t equals phi t after j zero is the reason the derivative with respect to t can be rewritten as a Lie derivative.

title: Integration Along Fibres
notes: Make the degree shift explicit. The operator first inserts the interval direction into eta, so a k-form becomes a k minus one form on each slice. Then the pullback to M removes the cylinder coordinate and the integral averages those slice contributions from zero to one. This is not ordinary integration of a scalar function; it is integration after contraction with the homotopy direction.

title: Lemma A.1: Boundary Equals Commutator
notes: Present Lemma A.1 as the de Rham version of the fundamental theorem of calculus. The left side is endpoint change. The right side is what Cartan's formula makes endpoint change become after we integrate the Lie derivative: one term where d falls outside the integral and one term where d first hits eta. This identity is the engine that will later manufacture primitives.

title: Homotopic Maps Give Cochain Homotopies
notes: Move from the cylinder on M to any smooth homotopy. Pull a form on the target back to the cylinder, apply the same I operator, and obtain H equals I after h star. The square is meant to be read algebraically: H is not a map between spaces, but a degree minus one operator between de Rham complexes whose boundary is the difference of the endpoint pullbacks.

title: Two Meanings Of Vanishing
notes: Slow down on terminology because this is where many mistakes enter. Pullback zero only tests tangent vectors that lie in the submanifold. Vanishing on the submanifold is stronger: the form must vanish on all ambient tangent directions based at the submanifold. Second-order vanishing is stronger again for the primitive; it says the coefficients and their first derivatives disappear along the submanifold.

title: Vector Bundle Setup
notes: Now place the abstract homotopy in the vector bundle. The zero section sits inside E, projection pi remembers the base point, and radial scaling moves each vector inside its own fibre. The slide shows the scaling c t of e equals t e for intuition, while the proof uses the reversed path h t equals c one minus t so that h zero is the identity and h one is sigma zero after pi.

title: Generalised Poincare Lemma Proof
notes: This is the main proof slide. Apply the cochain homotopy formula to the fibre contraction. With the proof orientation, the endpoint at t one is pi star sigma zero star and the endpoint at t zero is the identity, giving eta equals pi star sigma zero star eta minus dH eta minus H d eta. If eta is closed and its pullback to the zero section is zero, the first and third terms vanish and eta equals d of minus H eta.

title: Why Second Order Appears
notes: Explain the strengthened conclusion without expanding every coordinate formula. Near the zero section, the contraction vector field has size proportional to the fibre coordinate. If eta itself vanishes on the submanifold in the stronger ambient sense, its coefficients also contribute a vanishing factor. The integrand defining H eta is therefore a product of two first-order vanishing quantities, which is second order along the zero section.

title: Submanifold Corollary
notes: Close by converting the vector-bundle statement back into the geometric form used in contact topology. A tubular neighborhood identifies directions normal to L with a neighborhood of L in M. Once that identification is made, the vector-bundle lemma applies to the normal directions. The recap should leave students with one portable sentence: local exactness near a submanifold comes from integrating the radial contraction homotopy.
